chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Abbas ibn Musa, from Yunus, from Suleiman ibn Salim, who said:

I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about a man who employed another man with specified expenses and dirhams, on the condition that he send him to a land. When he arrived, a man from his companions invited him to his house for a month or two months, and he attained with him what made him needless from the expenditure of the employer. So the employee looked at what would have been spent upon him during the month if he had not invited him, so the one who invited him had sufficed him. So from whose wealth is that sufficient expenditure? Is it from the wealth of the employee or from the wealth of the employer? He (peace be upon him) said: 'If it was in the interest of the employer, then it is from his wealth, and otherwise it is upon the employee.'

And (I asked) about a man who employed a man with specified expenses and did not explain anything, on the condition that he send him to another land. So whatever was from the provisions of the employee, from washing the clothes and the bath, upon whom is it? He said: 'Upon the employer.'
ai.seo_question: Who bears the cost of an employee's living expenses when sent on a business trip by the employer?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi elucidates the principles of *ujrah* (wages) and *nafaqah* (maintenance) in Shia commercial jurisprudence, emphasizing that financial liability is determined by the purpose of the expense relative to the employer's benefit. It establishes a nuanced distinction where incidental gains or savings derived from the employer's directive are attributed to the employer, while standard living costs remain the employee's burden unless explicitly agreed otherwise. This ruling reflects the Shia scholarly emphasis on fairness (*adl*) and the prevention of unjust enrichment (*istihlak*) in contractual obligations.
